item.title: Now is the easiest time in history to start a business. If you don't do it now, when else will the time come?
item.description:
Compared to ten years ago, today’s entrepreneurial environment has become freer and more convenient. Founders no longer need to rely on traditional resources; instead, they can launch projects quickly and at low cost using modern tools and the internet!

I. Entrepreneurship no longer requires a “big setup”

  • Past: Entrepreneurship required investors, co-founders, an office, and several months of funding support.
  • Present: These are no longer necessities. As long as you have the internet and some basic tools, one person can start.

II. Every step of entrepreneurship has a solution
item.content:encoded:
Compared to ten years ago, today’s entrepreneurial environment has become freer and more convenient. Founders no longer need to rely on traditional resources; instead, they can launch projects quickly and at low cost using modern tools and the internet!

I. Entrepreneurship no longer requires a “big setup”

  • Past: Entrepreneurship required investors, co-founders, an office, and several months of funding support.
  • Present: These are no longer necessities. As long as you have the internet and some basic tools, one person can start.

II. Every step of entrepreneurship has a solution

  • Want ideas? - Mine inspiration on Reddit, app store reviews.
  • Want customers? - Attract users by building a personal brand or community.
  • Want to develop a product? - Quickly build software using tools like Bolt, Cursor, Replit, Lovable.
  • Want to get paid? - Stripe Link helps you easily handle payments.
  • Want to promote your product? - Collaborate with niche creators and leverage their credibility for dissemination.
  • Want to optimize operations? - Achieve automation using AI tools like GPT-4o, Claude, Gumloop.
  • Need an office space? - A kitchen table at home + noise-canceling headphones is enough.
  • Need advice? - Listen to podcasts, or contact experts directly on social media.
  • Want to start? - Start with small projects, learn while doing.

III. The barrier to entry for entrepreneurship is almost zero

  • No restrictions: No gatekeepers, CVs (resumes), or licenses are needed.
  • Key elements: Only persistence, taste (or quality), and internet connection are required.
  • Learning opportunities: Entrepreneurial knowledge is available anytime (like a “24/7 open school”), and it’s free, but the real “tuition” is action—you must do it.

IV. Core message: Action is key Today’s entrepreneurs possess unprecedented resources and opportunities; there is no excuse not to start. The key to success lies in:

  • Act immediately: Start with small projects and accumulate experience.
  • Continuous effort: Persistence and learning are the path to success.

item.title: Breaking free from the control of money is financial freedom.
item.description: Explore the essence of money as life energy, guide readers to reflect on the value relationship between time and matter, and learn how to master one's own wealth.
item.content:encoded:
Money is what you exchange your life energy for. You sell time to acquire money. Ned sells time for $100 an hour, and you sell time for $20 an hour—that doesn’t matter. Ned’s money has nothing to do with you. The only true wealth you possess is your time, every second and minute of your life.

You use some of that precious time to exchange for money (cash), but money is meaningless; your time is where all meaning and value reside.

“Understanding that money is life energy will make you the master of money. You will clearly know how much life energy you are willing to sell to acquire money. Look around at what you have accumulated, and you can ask yourself: ‘How much time from my life did I invest to own this… chair… car… set of cookware… diploma on the wall?’ See how this affects your next purchase.”

item.title: Stock Market and Economy: Focus on the Owner Rather Than the Dog
item.description: Through vivid metaphors, explain the short-term fluctuations and long-term trends of the stock market, reminding investors to focus on economic fundamentals rather than short-term market changes.
item.content:encoded:
The stock market is like a very excited dog, which is tied to one end of a long leash. The owner holds the leash, and the dog sniffs randomly in all directions. Assuming in this example, the dog owner represents the economy, and he is walking in New York City, starting from the Columbus Circle, passing through Central Park, and arriving at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. From one second to the next, the dog might turn right or left; its movement cannot be precisely predicted.

However, in the long run, the dog’s direction of movement is not mysterious; just like the owner, this dog is moving northeast at a speed of approximately 3 miles per hour.

Surprisingly, almost all people tracking the market are focusing on the dog, rather than the dog owner.

item.title: Never buy things from panting people.
item.description: Explore the investment wisdom of Burton Malkiel and Warren Buffett, emphasizing the importance of avoiding high management fees and overconfidence.
item.content:encoded:
Merton Malkiel’s saying: “Never buy from a panting person.”

Warren Buffett also said something similar: “Be wary of investment activities that make people cheer; true investment genius is usually very boring.”

When trillions of dollars are managed by Wall Street professionals and charge high management fees, it is usually the managers who reap huge profits, not the clients.

Don’t assume you know more than the market; no one knows more than the market. Don’t act based on your own opinions; you think that is your idea alone, but in reality, millions of people think that way."

The lower the annual fee paid by investors, the more money left in their pocket.

item.title: How to acquire customers through international marketing?
item.description: This article introduces how to build an efficient AI-driven content marketing system through user research, content creation, multi-platform distribution, and automated optimization.
item.content:encoded:
User Research and Insights

By conducting in-depth research around Reddit using multiple AI tools (such as Gemini 2.5, Deepresearch, Grok 3, Perplexity), with a specific focus on user complaints and comments. Four independent reports are generated to summarize authentic user feedback, providing data support for subsequent content creation.

Building Content Ecosystem and SEO Optimization

Based on the excavated user complaints, issues are refined and converted into topics. Articles are written focusing on experience sharing and solutions, and combined with Search Engine Optimization (SEO) strategies, integrating high-frequency search terms into the content. These are published on the website blog to ensure the content has high potential for search ranking.

Multi-Platform Variant Creation and Distribution

Around the published SEO content, variant formats suitable for different platforms are created:

  • Twitter: Repurposed into Threads.
  • Medium: Compressed into short-form articles.
  • Reddit: Converted into first-person stories or Ask Me Anything (AMA) posts.
  • Instagram/Pinterest: Designed as visual image/text content.
  • TikTok/Youtube Shorts: Produced as short video versions.

When published on each platform, the platform’s recommendation algorithm is utilized to boost content visibility, ensuring maximum search weight.

Content Traffic Generation and User Conversion

After publishing on multiple platforms, clear Calls to Action (CTAs) are added to guide traffic back to the SEO landing page. High-quality content attracts visitors and encourages them to leave their email addresses to complete registration.

Continuous Iteration and Optimization

Data from the SEO landing page is regularly organized and analyzed to identify the top 20% performing content. Fine-grained operations are implemented for this high-quality content, such as:

  • Seeking influencer collaborations on TikTok.
  • Running paid advertisements to expand influence.
  • Utilizing Instagram and Pinterest to strengthen image marketing effects.

The Turning Point for Explosive Growth

Growth is typically linear until a “fulcrum” is found; however, once this critical threshold is broken, the business will experience exponential growth. Therefore, it is essential to concentrate resources on the core content and drive its widespread dissemination.

Automation and Scaling

Repetitive tasks within the above workflow are handed over to an Agent system, achieving comprehensive automation of content marketing. Ultimately, an AI Native Marketing Agency is built.

item.title: From Zero to One: My Independent App Journey
item.description: Sharing my experience developing my first independent app, including choosing a niche market, the listing process, and the dilemma when facing feature upgrades.
item.content:encoded:
From Zero to One: My Solo App Journey

After a week of tinkering, my first independently developed APP is finally live! It’s priced at $9.99, and it sold two copies on the second day. This is a brand new start for me, and a new revenue stream has begun 🥳🥳🥳

Choosing a Niche Market

I specifically chose a very niche market with almost no competitors—it could be called a blank slate. Of course, the demand isn’t high, and it’s not a hot application field. But looking at it from another angle, this might be the perfect place for a beginner to practice 🤠

The Dilemma of Feature Upgrades

Right now, I am facing a dilemma: Should I add some more advanced features to this APP? This definitely carries a big risk. If handled improperly, it could easily lead to app crashes and significantly diminish the user experience 😡

This question has made me think about it for a long time. On the one hand, adding features can attract more users and boost competitiveness; on the other hand, I am worried about the technical challenges and potential risks. You might have experienced a similar dilemma, right? What would you choose?

No matter what, this is a journey full of challenges and hope. I will continue to work hard and constantly improve this APP, making it a proud piece of my work. 🥳🥳🥳🥳🥳

item.title: One of the business mindsets: Focusing on others
item.description: An excellent businessman knows how to approach interactions centered on others, building influence through caring for and understanding them, rather than constantly boasting about oneself. This kind of business mindset is the key to success.
item.content:encoded:
The Basic Potential of an Excellent Merchant

Always maintain interest in others, focus your interest and energy on them, center your topics around others, and conduct your interactions revolving around other people.

Achieving this while also managing the boundaries—asking questions that everyone feels comfortable with, rather than feeling constantly probed and uncomfortable—is very difficult.

The Vast Majority Cannot Learn to Be Other-Centered

Caring about others, being interested in others, understanding others.

They are only interested in themselves, only centered on themselves, only willing to understand themselves, unwilling to understand others, and only want to influence others, allowing others to understand themselves. But this will not achieve your goals.

If You Want to Influence Others, Infect Others, and Change Them

The first step is not to obsessively sell or boast about yourself, but rather to constantly understand others, to be other-centered, allowing others to feel valued. Then, during and after this process, you subtly exert your influence.

This mindset might be called Business Thinking. Whereas being only interested in yourself, only centered on yourself, only willing to understand yourself, having no interest in others, and not wanting to understand others—this might be called Loser Thinking.

item.title: Free Temptation: Reconstructing Consumer Value Judgments Through Price Zeroing
item.description: By utilizing methods such as price anchoring, psychological account resetting, and social currency creation, design a complete user growth and retention plan to achieve a business closed-loop of acquiring high-value users at zero cost.
item.content:encoded:
I. Price Anchor Reconstruction (Anchoring Effect + Psychological Account Reset)

  1. App Store Pricing Strategy
  • List at a high price of $99.99/year (actual price never discounted)
  • Product description emphasizes “Enterprise-grade Service” and “Original Price for Institutional Procurement Only”
  • Feature list uses B-end terminology such as “Enterprise Security Solution” and “Million-level Data Processing”
  1. Cognitive Framework Conversion
  • Publish a “User Benefit Upgrade Announcement” on the official website/social media:
  • “To celebrate users reaching 100,000, we are temporarily opening the personal free channel (Original Price $99.99 → 0 Yuan)”
  • Set a countdown timer: Display remaining free slots (dynamic fake data, always maintaining <10% availability)

II. Zero-Price Trigger Design (Dual-Channel Loss Aversion)

  1. Registration Code Acquisition Mechanism
  • Design a “Golden Invitation Code” system:
  • Unlock Enterprise Edition features valued at $99.99 (limited to individual users) Set up a dual loss framework: ✅ Claim Immediately → Gain VIP privileges worth $99.99 (Permanent) ❌ Decline Claim → Lose the maximum annual benefit (Red text warning)
  1. Sunk Cost Implantation
  • Obtaining the invitation code requires completing three steps:
    1. Enter mobile number to get verification code (Initiating commitment consistency)
    2. Watch 15-second product video (Attention sinking)
    3. Select three interest tags (Personalized anchoring)

III. Social Currency Creation (Viral Spread Engine)

  1. Vanity Sharing Design
  • Automatically generate a “Digital Asset Report” after successful registration:
  • “You have saved $99.99, surpassing 92% of users”
  • The sharing page includes:
  • Dynamic ranking bar: “Your free code value exceeds XX people”
  • Virtual badge: “Savvy Decision Maker,” “0 Yuan Challenge Success”
  1. Group Behavior Stimulation
  • Create a “Limited-Time Free Alliance” leaderboard:
  • Invite 1 person to gain “Credit Stars,” which can be exchanged for an extended free period
  • The top 100 display real user avatars, triggering competitive psychology

IV. Scarcity Maintenance System (Dynamic Fake Resources)

  1. Multi-Dimensional Scarcity Prompts
  • Geographic Fencing Technology: “Only 43 free slots remain in Chaoyang District, Beijing where you are located”
  • Device Recognition Prompt: “iOS user exclusive quota is about to run out”
  • Ghost Inventory Strategy: Real-time display of “Users Currently Claiming”

Example Algorithm (Actual data needs to be faked/simulated)

import random
current_users = random.randint(87, 92) # Always display 90% claim rate
remaining = 1000 - current_users

V. Neural Reward Circuit Construction (Dopamine Pulse System)

  1. Unscheduled Surprise Rewards
  • Trigger “Gold Coin Rain” animation when the user first opens the APP
  • Randomly drop tangible rewards (requires completing a specified action to claim): “Congratulations! Invite 1 more person to redeem a Starbucks coupon”
  • “Click to claim: Free extension of 3 days of premium features”
  1. Progress Bar Addiction Design
  • Personal Center sets up “Privilege Unlock Progress”: 2% progress bar increase upon daily login
  • When reaching 80% prompt: “Free qualification is about to be lost, invite a friend immediately to freeze progress”

VI. Behavioral Trace Conversion (Endowment Effect Activation)

  1. Virtual Asset Accumulation
  • Automatically create a “Personal Data Center” for the user
  • Even if not actively used, it generates: “We have analyzed 1,302 potential connections for you”
  • “3 important schedules detected awaiting activation”
  1. Loss Visualization Reminder
  • Push notification triggered after three days of inactivity: “Your free benefits are flowing away! Accumulated value of $8.33 unused”
  • Coupled with virtual currency visualization: “Account Balance: $99.99 → Log in now to stop the loss”

VII. Moral License Backdoor (Cognitive Dissonance Elimination)

  1. Legitimacy Endorsement Construction
  • Add to the bottom of the registration page: “For every free code claimed, we donate 1 minute of digital education to mountainous regions”

  1. Decision Rationalization Script Confirmation Pop-up Design:

  2. “You are making a wise choice:

  3. ✔ Saving $99.99 in personal expenses

  4. ✔ Supporting the cause of educational equity

  5. ✔ Joining the 100,000 elite community”

Enhanced Effect Combination Punch

  1. Cross-Platform Cognitive Bombardment
  • Create a question on Zhihu: “What is the experience of claiming XX free codes?”
  • Initiate a “Free Code Exchange” pseudo-user topic on Douban Group
  • Layout the keyword “How to get XX Golden Invitation Code” on WeChat Search
  1. Physical World Touchpoints
  • Distribute “Free Code Coffee Cup Sleeves” at coffee chains
  • Set up “Scan Code Free Printing” terminals in university towns
  • Partner with parcel lockers to pop up advertisements: “Collect items and claim digital benefits for free”

Through this scheme, you will create a self-reinforcing behavioral magnetic field: Zero-price trigger for initial acquisition → Social display forms secondary spread → Fake scarcity promotes urgent action → Neural rewards maintain continuous participation. The key is maintaining the state of “High Value - Zero Cost” cognitive imbalance, keeping the rational evaluation system continuously suppressed.

item.title: Foundational Theories of Communication
item.description: This paper reviews the foundational theories of communication studies, including 23 important theories such as Agenda-setting theory, Spiral of Silence theory, and Uses and Gratifications theory. It provides a detailed introduction to the originator, core concepts, and specific explanations of each theory.
item.content:encoded:
Review of Fundamental Theories of Communication

1. Agenda-Setting Theory

Proponents: Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw
Core Idea: Media influences the public’s ranking of issues by selecting and emphasizing certain topics.
Explanation: What the media reports, the public tends to pay more attention to. For example, if the media constantly reports on climate change, people may perceive climate change as one of the most important current issues.

2. Spiral of Silence Theory

Proponents: Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann
Core Idea: People fear being isolated for expressing minority views, so they choose to remain silent, which in turn makes the mainstream views appear stronger.
Explanation: In a social setting, if someone supports an unpopular policy, they might choose not to express their opinion for fear of being ridiculed or excluded.

3. Uses and Gratifications Theory

Proponents: Elihu Katz et al.
Core Idea: Audiences actively choose media to satisfy their needs, such as gaining information, entertainment, or establishing social connections.
Explanation: For instance, some watch the news to get current affairs information, while others scroll through short videos for relaxation and entertainment.

4. Two-Step Flow of Communication Theory

Proponents: Paul Lazarsfeld et al.
Core Idea: Information first influences Opinion Leaders, and then those leaders pass the information on to ordinary people.
Explanation: A celebrity (Opinion Leader) shares their view on a certain brand of phone, and fans may consequently be more inclined to purchase that brand’s phone.

5. Media Dependency Theory

Proponents: Sandra Ball-Rokeach and Melvin DeFleur
Core Idea: The degree to which people depend on the media determines the media’s influence on them.
Explanation: During a natural disaster, people rely more heavily on news media for information, significantly enhancing the media’s influence.

6. Cultivation Theory

Proponents: George Gerbner
Core Idea: Long-term exposure to certain types of media content influences people’s worldview, leading to a distorted perception of the real world.
Explanation: If someone watches violent movies for a long time, they might perceive the real world as being more violent than it actually is.

7. Framing Theory

Proponents: Erving Goffman et al.
Core Idea: Media shapes how audiences understand events through specific organizational and presentation methods.
Explanation: For example, regarding the same protest, the media can present it through two different frames—“peaceful demonstration” or “violent conflict”—leading to vastly different audience interpretations.

8. Diffusion of Innovations Theory

Proponents: Everett Rogers
Core Idea: The spread of innovation occurs in different stages, influenced by early adopters, social networks, and cultural background.
Explanation: After a new smartwatch is launched, early adopters purchase and use it first, subsequently influencing their friends and family to join the purchasing ranks.

9. Media Ecology Theory

Proponents: Marshall McLuhan et al.
Core Idea: Media, as a technological form of information transmission, profoundly influences social culture and behavior.
Explanation: McLuhan’s concept of “The Medium is the Message” suggests that different media forms themselves shape people’s communication methods and thought habits. For instance, the television era emphasizes visual expression, while the book era emphasizes textual logic.

10. Cultural Hegemony Theory

Proponents: Antonio Gramsci
Core Idea: Through cultural transmission, the social elite can maintain control over ideology.
Explanation: Mainstream movies and TV programs often consolidate existing social values through narrative, such as promoting individual striving and consumerism.

11. Knowledge Gap Theory

Proponents: Philip Tichenor et al.
Core Idea: Information disseminated by the media often exacerbates the information gap between high-knowledge and low-knowledge groups.
Explanation: For example, the spread of scientific news might make educated people more knowledgeable about related topics, while those with lower education levels may feel even more unfamiliar with them.

12. Third-Person Effect Theory

Proponents: W. Phillips Davison
Core Idea: People tend to believe that media content influences others more strongly than it influences themselves, and they take certain actions in response.
Explanation: For instance, some believe that advertisements strongly influence others to buy things, but not themselves, so they might advocate for stricter regulation of advertising.

13. The Strength of Weak Ties Theory

Proponents: Mark Granovetter
Core Idea: In social networks, “weak ties” (acquaintanceship) are more effective than “strong ties” (close ties) in spreading information and facilitating resource flow.
Explanation: A casual friend might provide you with important job information because the information they encounter is different from your immediate circle, whereas close friends usually share similar information with you.

14. Double Reality Theory

Proponents: Nikki K. R. Kroeber et al.
Core Idea: Media reports often construct the relationship between reality (what the media presents) and social reality (what people actually experience) simultaneously.
Explanation: For example, people perceive a high crime rate from media reports, but in their own daily lives, they rarely encounter crime directly.

15. Gap Model of Information Seeking

Proponents: Robert S. Taylor
Core Idea: Information seeking behavior stems from the “information gap” between a perceived problem and current knowledge.
Explanation: When someone learns that a company might go bankrupt but doesn’t know the specific reasons, they might actively search for related information to bridge that gap.

16. Media Richness Theory

Proponents: Richard L. Daft and Robert H. Lengel
Core Idea: Different media possess varying degrees of information richness; complex information requires transmission through rich media.
Explanation: Face-to-face interaction is the richest form of media, while written text is relatively poor; therefore, complex negotiations are better suited for face-to-face interaction rather than email.

17. Social Comparison Theory

Proponents: Leon Festinger
Core Idea: People evaluate their own opinions and abilities by comparing themselves to others, and the media intensifies this comparison.
Explanation: On social media, after seeing others’ successful lives (like vacation photos), people might feel that they are not as successful or happy.

18. Uses and Dependency Model

Proponents: Sandra Ball-Rokeach and Melvin DeFleur
Core Idea: Media influence depends on the individual’s degree of dependency on media information and the strength of the social system.
Explanation: During a large-scale internet outage, people’s dependency on social media may expose critical vulnerabilities within the communication system.

19. Selective Exposure Theory

Proponents: Joseph Klapper
Core Idea: People tend to choose media information that aligns with their existing views while avoiding information that contradicts them.
Explanation: A political partisan might more frequently watch news channels that align with their party’s stance.

20. Fourth Estate Theory

Proponents: Edmund Burke
Core Idea: The media, as an independent social institution, plays the role of supervising and balancing power.
Explanation: Investigative journalism that exposes government corruption or corporate misconduct embodies the media’s role as the “Fourth Estate.”

21. Perceptual Filter Theory

Proponents: Harold Lasswell
Core Idea: During the process of information transmission, people’s background, preferences, and experiences influence how they receive and understand information.
Explanation: The same piece of news might be interpreted as a positive signal by an optimist, while a pessimist might view it as a negative warning.

22. Information Overload Theory

Proponents: Alvin Toffler
Core Idea: When information exceeds human processing capacity, it can lead to decision difficulty, decreased efficiency, or even anxiety.
Explanation: When shopping on an e-commerce platform, faced with hundreds of similar products, people may find it harder to make a purchasing decision.

23. Media Logic Theory

Proponents: David Altheide and Robert Snow
Core Idea: The way media is presented and its underlying logic profoundly influence societal ways of thinking and behavioral patterns.
Explanation: Television programs often use an entertainment logic, which causes news reporting to tend toward attracting viewers through entertainment rather than deep analysis.

item.title: Human weaknesses exploited by streamers
item.description: This article delves into various human weaknesses, such as greed, laziness, and jealousy, and analyzes how influencers utilize these psychological traits to attract traffic and build influence. The aim is to help readers understand the operational logic of the online ecosystem and remain vigilant.
item.content:encoded:
Human Weaknesses:

  • Greed: The infinite craving for wealth, profit, and benefits, making people easily attracted to temptations like “quick riches,” “insider information,” and “low-risk, high-return” opportunities. Influencers utilize giveaways, benefits, and “secret” investment tips to cater to this psychology.

  • Sloth: The unwillingness to put in effort, craving easy attainment of success, happiness, knowledge, etc. The content provided by influencers—such as “learn in one click,” “easy weight loss,” or “passive income techniques”—directly exploits this tendency.

  • Hypocrisy: Saying one thing but meaning another; concealing true thoughts to maintain an image or benefit. Influencers may package their persona or engage in false advertising, and some audiences will selectively believe what they wish to believe.

  • Need for Face/Prestige: Valuing one’s image in the eyes of others, fearing embarrassment, and craving respect and admiration. Influencers create a “high-class” image or satisfy vanity by posting “check-ins” and “showing off.”

  • Competitiveness: The desire to surpass others and gain a sense of superiority, fearing being surpassed. Influencers may create conflict or spark discussions, triggering “defending the idol” behavior among fans.

  • Schadenfreude/Enjoying Others’ Misfortune: Finding secret pleasure in the misfortune of others. The traffic generated by an influencer’s “fall from grace,” negative news, or controversial events is partly due to catering to this dark psychology.

  • Lust: A strong craving for sensory stimulation, especially sexual. Some influencers attract attention through suggestive or vulgar content.

  • Pride/Arrogance: Having an inflated sense of self-worth, being resistant to different opinions, and easily being charmed by flattery and praise. Influencers may cultivate a “superior” posture, and some audiences enjoy worshipping this “master.”

  • Envy: Feeling dissatisfaction or pain because others possess what one desires. The superior lifestyle displayed by influencers may trigger envy in some people, but it can also transform into attention.

  • Anger/Hatred: Intense negative emotions that are easily incited and exploited. Influencers may attract traffic by creating conflict or attacking specific groups.

  • Fear: Worry about danger, the unknown, or loss. Influencers create anxiety and sensationalize crises, then offer a “solution” (which is often a product or service).

  • Fear of the Unknown/Superstition: People feel uneasy about phenomena they cannot explain or about the future, making them prone to believing superstitions or seeking psychological comfort. Some influencers utilize content like horoscopes, tarot cards, and Feng Shui to cater to this psychology.

  • Fear of Death: Although rarely mentioned directly, the fear of aging, illness, and death drives people to focus on health and longevity secrets. Influencers may provide related products or information.

  • Need for Belonging/Affiliation: Craving to be a part of a group and gain recognition and support. Influencers build fan communities, emphasizing shared values and goals to increase fan loyalty.

  • Excessive Sympathy/Savior Complex: Over-sympathizing with the weak or victims, making people easily moved by sentimental stories or pleas for help. Influencers may use this for marketing or guidance.

  • Hyper-Conformity: Not just following the crowd, but sacrificing one’s independent thought and judgment to fit in with the group. The “trends” or “hot topics” created by influencers easily lead some people to blindly follow.

  • Cognitive Miserliness: The tendency to use simple ways of thinking and avoid complex thought. The information disseminated by influencers is often simplified and labeled, catering to this psychology.

  • Reinforcement of Confirmation Bias: People tend to accept and believe information that aligns with their existing beliefs. Influencers cater to this by providing content that confirms the fans’ existing knowledge, strengthening their biases.

  • Desire for Simple Answers: When facing complex problems, people tend to seek simple, direct answers, even if those answers are not comprehensive or accurate. The “solve it in one move” or “learn in three steps” content provided by influencers exploits this.

  • Need for Certainty: People dislike uncertainty and hope that things are predictable and controllable. Influencers may provide “predictions” or “analyses” that seem to bring certainty.

  • Novelty Seeking: People are easily bored with repetitive content and crave new, stimulating, and unusual things. Influencers must constantly create new content and topics to maintain appeal.

  • Desire for Easy Pleasure: People tend to seek simple, direct pleasures, such as entertainment or sensory stimulation. The funny videos and lighthearted skits provided by influencers satisfy this need.

  • Escapism: The desire to temporarily escape the pressures and troubles of reality. The entertainment content and fictional stories provided by influencers can satisfy this need.

  • Need for Control: People wish to have a certain degree of control over their lives and environment. In a world of information overload, choosing which influencers to follow and which comments to post becomes a way of expressing control.

  • Preference for Stories and Narratives: People are more likely to accept and remember information presented in a story format. Influencers attract audiences by sharing personal experiences or fabricating stories.

  • Desire to be Understood and Valued: Everyone hopes their thoughts, feelings, and experiences are understood and recognized by others. Influencers cater to this need by sharing personal stories, expressing views similar to those of their fans, and even seemingly “listening” to fan comments, making fans feel “seen.”

  • Tendency towards Group Polarization: When people gather with those who share similar views, their views tend to become more extreme. Influencers create an “echo chamber,” reinforcing the shared cognition of fans and inciting conflict, thereby strengthening fan loyalty.

  • Desire for Participation and Control: Even small actions, such as liking, commenting, or voting, can give people a sense of participation and a degree of control. Influencers utilize polls, comment section interactions, and challenges to make fans feel like they are part of the content creation process.

  • Admiration for “Success” and “Elites”: People are easily attracted to those who display success or elite status and crave learning their “secrets.” Influencers deliberately cultivate a glamorous image and share “success experiences,” even if those experiences are not real or universal.

  • Obsession with “Insider Information”: People believe that possessing information others don’t know brings an advantage. Influencers create the illusion of “exclusive leaks” or “insider information,” making fans feel they possess some kind of privilege.

  • Cognitive Inertia from Information Echo Chambers: When long-term immersed in an information echo chamber, people become increasingly resistant to information that contradicts their views, becoming more stubborn. Influencers intensify the echo chamber effect through precise recommendations, making it easier for fans to accept the content they are exposed to.

  • Blind Faith in Authority: Even if the influencer is not a professional, once they gain a certain level of attention in a field, they are easily viewed as an “authority.” Fans are more likely to believe what they say, even if that information lacks scientific basis.

  • Moral Superiority: People like to feel they are standing on a moral high ground; criticizing or blaming others brings a sense of superiority. Influencers attract traffic by creating “moral role models” or attacking “morally corrupt” behavior, allowing fans to resonate with them.

  • Desire for “Rebellion” and “Individuality” (Even Performative): Especially among younger demographics, striving to be different is a common psychological drive. Influencers may attract audiences who crave self-expression by adopting a “anti-traditional” or “revealing the truth” stance, even if this “rebellion” is carefully packaged.

  • Need for Companionship and Emotional Comfort: In a society where loneliness is increasing, the seemingly friendly interactions and positive image of influencers can provide emotional comfort and companionship for some people.

  • Overzealous Pursuit of “Sincerity” and “Authenticity” (Sometimes Deceived by Feigned Sincerity): People crave seeing genuine humanity, but they are also easily deceived by carefully designed “sincerity.” Influencers create an “authentic” image by showcasing “flaws” or “mistakes.”

  • Desire to be Heard and Have a Voice: For those at the bottom of society, effective channels for expression are often lacking. The influencer platform provides a seemingly accessible platform to express one’s views and gain attention. They may participate in the influencer’s “power game” through comments and likes, as if they too possess a certain influence.

  • Seeing Influencers as “Spokespersons” or “Saviors”: Some ordinary people may view influencers as “spokespersons” who can represent their interests or even hope that they can change their circumstances, generating a sense of illusory power.

  • Gaining a Sense of Collective Power Through “Taking Sides” and “Supporting”: Ordinary people may feel powerless in real life, but online, by supporting a certain influencer and participating in the fan group’s “battle,” they gain a sense of collective power and belonging.

  • Greed: This can be analyzed in more detail across different forms of greed, such as the craving for material wealth, the desire for the halo of “success,” or even the desire for information possession.

  • Need for Face/Prestige: This can emphasize how influencers utilize the “hierarchy of contempt” effect, allowing some fans to gain a sense of superiority by following them.

  • Competitiveness: This is not only reflected in the “defending the idol” among fans but also in maintaining and competing for the influencer’s own “status.”

  • Fear: This can be analyzed more specifically regarding the types of anxiety created by influencers, such as appearance anxiety, body anxiety, class anxiety, and knowledge anxiety.

  • Hyper-Conformity: This can emphasize how influencers utilize the “herd mentality” and the “bandwagon fallacy” to guide fan behavior.

  • Reinforcement of Confirmation Bias: This can analyze how influencers strengthen fans’ inherent beliefs by selectively presenting information and blocking dissenting opinions.

Summary:

These human weaknesses are complex and interconnected, deeply rooted in our genes and culture. Successful influencers are often able to keenly capture these weaknesses and skillfully utilize them to attract traffic, build influence, and even achieve commercial monetization. When we conduct this thought experiment, it is not to criticize humanity, but to gain a deeper understanding of the operating logic of the online ecosystem and to remind ourselves to remain vigilant, avoiding manipulation by these weaknesses. Just as you said, this is like Einstein’s elevator thought experiment—aimed at exploring deep-seated laws, rather than encouraging immoral behavior.

item.content:encoded:
In life, there are always some seemingly ordinary things that contain profound philosophical meanings. Take bees and sweetness as an example; we may rarely think about the story behind it. Bees are hardworking creatures in nature, diligently collecting nectar to transform it into sweet delicacies. These sweets then become delightful treats for people, allowing them to savor happiness.

However, if we delve deeper, we might discover that there seems to be something hidden between the bees’ hard work and the sweetness enjoyed by humans. Perhaps there is a subtle yet profound implication behind this. We can recall scenes that seem familiar.

Once upon a time, there was a place where people lived an ordinary life but felt the invisible pressure from above. They were required to put in more effort, working silently for so-called ‘happiness.’ These people, like bees, worked hard, transforming their sweat and labor into what they believed was ‘sweetness,’ but did that ‘sweetness’ truly belong to them?

Those at the top perhaps didn’t exert the same effort as the bees for this ‘sweetness.’ Yet, due to some force, they enjoyed the ‘sweetness’ gained through others’ efforts, seemingly justified. And people, perhaps accustomed to such lives, endured their inner frustration, continuing to strive for that ‘sweetness,’ as if the meaning of life lay solely in this ‘sweetness.’

But if we return to the story of the bees again, we might find clues for reflection. Although bees work hard, they also create their own lives while contributing to ecological balance. People should also consider whether, while pursuing apparent ‘sweetness,’ they can create more possibilities for themselves and bring more beauty to society.

When looking at those who are seen as ‘bees,’ we should also pay more attention to whether they receive the respect and fairness they deserve while working. In such reflections, we can view the so-called ‘sweetness’ and its underlying values more objectively. After all, without the hard work of bees, how could there be sweetness? Every effort in life deserves proper reward, not just fleeting, illusory ‘sweetness.’ +++

When dealing with risk management, there are many useful tools and methods that can help you reduce financial risks and better manage your assets. Here are some risk management tools and methods worth considering:

  1. Insurance: Purchasing appropriate insurance is the most basic and important risk management tool. Health insurance, car insurance, property insurance, life insurance, etc., can provide you with economic support and protection when accidents or disasters occur.

  2. Diversified Portfolio: When investing, spreading funds across different asset classes, such as stocks, bonds, real estate, and cash, helps to diversify risk. Such a diversified portfolio can reduce losses when specific assets perform poorly.

  3. Emergency Savings Fund: Establishing an emergency savings fund is used to cope with sudden emergencies and unexpected expenses. It is usually recommended to save an amount equivalent to three to six months of living expenses as an emergency reserve.

  4. Stop-Loss Strategy: In investing, setting a stop-loss point is a common risk management method. By setting a price point, assets are automatically sold when the asset price falls to a certain degree, thus avoiding further losses.

  5. Professional Financial Advisor: Seeking the help of a professional financial advisor or wealth planner can help you formulate personalized risk management strategies and make reasonable plans based on your goals and risk tolerance.

  6. Long-Term Investment: Long-term investment is usually more stable than short-term speculation because it can smoothly handle market fluctuations and achieve more stable returns through the accumulation of time.

  7. Healthy Lifestyle: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle helps reduce medical costs and health risks. Regular physical examinations and maintaining healthy eating habits can reduce the possibility of illness.

  8. Compliance with Laws and Regulations: Adhering to laws and regulations, including traffic rules and building safety standards, can reduce many potential property and liability risks.

  9. Education Planning: Planning for your children’s education in advance helps to distribute the pressure of future educational expenses.

  10. Debt Management: Managing personal debt ensures that the debt burden is reasonable and does not exceed your capacity to bear it.

In summary, risk management is a crucial part of personal financial planning. By using appropriate tools and methods, you can better protect your and your family’s financial security and plan for the future more effectively.

item.title: How to start an app business with no money?

  • Consider crowdfunding. Run a Kickstarter campaign to fund development costs and assess demand.

item.content:encoded:
Work is the essence of human life, but it is not the purpose of human life. The author argues that from the moment humans appeared on Earth, they have had to engage in labor to acquire resources and energy, thereby sustaining survival and reproduction. However, work is not the sole meaning of human existence; humans also have other needs and pursuits, such as leisure, entertainment, social interaction, and creativity. The author calls on us not to treat work as a religion (or faith), but rather as a means to better enjoy life.

The form and meaning of work change as human civilization evolves. The author traces the historical transformation of human labor, from primitive society, agricultural society, industrial society, to modern society. He points out that different social forms and economic systems have different definitions and requirements for work. In primitive society, people did not have the concept of “work”; they simply labored to meet basic survival needs. In agricultural society, people began to settle down and cultivate land, forming land ownership and class systems. In industrial society, people were alienated into “tool people” (or “cogs in the machine”), working tirelessly for economic growth. In modern society, people have greater expectations and challenges regarding work, hoping to gain a sense of value and achievement through it.

Scarcity economics is the root cause of people’s overworking. The author believes that the “scarcity mindset” prevalent in modern society makes people worry that resources are insufficient, thus striving hard to work to acquire more wealth and material goods. However, this mindset ignores that human demand for resources is finite, and resources themselves are not fixed or unchanging. The author proposes the concept of “Abundance Economics” (or “Sufficiency Economics”), arguing that humans should learn from primitive society how to control desires, be content with existing resources, and expand the availability of resources through innovation and collaboration.

Automation technology will bring new opportunities and challenges to humanity. The author predicts that in the future, robots will replace humans in performing most repetitive and low-skilled jobs, which will lead humans to face crises of unemployment and uselessness. But at the same time, this will also bring new possibilities to humanity, giving people more time and space to develop fields they are interested in and skilled at, and creating more valuable and meaningful work. The author suggests that we should rethink the question of “what makes us human,” and transition from being “tool people” to being “Human Beings.”

With your username and avatar exposed countless times, some people will inevitably click on them. By posting business-related videos and leaving your personal WeChat in the signature, people will add you as a friend daily, resulting in a very stable conversion rate.

The specific steps for beginners are as follows:

  1. Find a niche industry that has high conversion rates, is a necessity (high demand), and has a wide market.
  2. Organize relevant materials.
  3. Register a D Account, modify the username and avatar, post a few business-related videos, and use the signature to guide people to add your WeChat.

Essentially, you’re working for somebody else, and that person is taking on the risk and has the accountability, the intellectual property, and the brand. They’re not going to pay you enough. They’re going to pay you the bare minimum they have to, to get you to do their job. That can be a high bare minimum, but it’s still not going to be true wealth where you’re retired but still earning. [78] Owning equity in a company basically means you own the upside. When you own debt, you own guaranteed revenue streams and you own the downside. You want to own equity. If you don’t own equity in a business, your odds of making money are very slim. You have to work up to the point where you can own equity in a business. You could own equity as a small shareholder where you bought stock. You could also own it as an owner where you started the company. Ownership is really important.

item.description:

Pick an industry where you can play long-term games with long-term people.

The internet has massively broadened the possible space of careers. Most people haven’t figured this out yet.

↓ Play iterated games. All the returns in life, whether in wealth, relationships, or knowledge, come from compound interest.
↓ Pick business partners with high intelligence, energy, and, above all, integrity.
↓ Don’t partner with cynics and pessimists. Their beliefs are self-fulfilling.
↓ Learn to sell. Learn to build. If you can do both, you will be unstoppable.
↓ Arm yourself with specific knowledge, accountability, and leverage.
↓ Specific knowledge is knowledge you cannot be trained for. If society can train you, it can train someone else and replace you.
↓ Specific knowledge is found by pursuing your genuine curiosity and passion rather than whatever is hot right now.
↓ Building specific knowledge will feel like play to you but will look like work to others.
↓ When specific knowledge is taught, it’s through apprenticeships, not schools.
↓ Specific knowledge is often highly technical or creative. It cannot be outsourced or automated.
↓ Embrace accountability, and take business risks under your own name. Society will reward you with responsibility, equity, and leverage.
↓ “Give me a lever long enough and a place to stand, and I will move the earth.” —Archimedes
↓ Fortunes require leverage. Business leverage comes from capital, people, and products with no marginal cost of replication (code and media).
↓ Capital means money. To raise money, apply your specific knowledge with accountability and show resulting good judgment.
↓ Labor means people working for you. It’s the oldest and most fought-over form of leverage. Labor leverage will impress your parents, but don’t waste your life chasing it.
↓ Capital and labor are permissioned leverage. Everyone is chasing capital, but someone has to give it to you. Everyone is trying to lead, but someone has to follow you.
↓ Code and media are permissionless leverage. They’re the leverage behind the newly rich. You can create software and media that works for you while you sleep.
↓ An army of robots is freely available—it’s just packed in data centers for heat and space efficiency. Use it.
↓ If you can’t code, write books and blogs, record videos and podcasts.
↓ Leverage is a force multiplier for your judgment.
↓ Judgment requires experience but can be built faster by learning foundational skills.
↓ There is no skill called “business.” Avoid business magazines and business classes.
↓ Study microeconomics, game theory, psychology, persuasion, ethics, mathematics, and computers.
↓ Reading is faster than listening. Doing is faster than watching.
↓ You should be too busy to “do coffee” while still keeping an uncluttered calendar.
↓ Set and enforce an aspirational personal hourly rate. If fixing a problem will save less than your hourly rate, ignore it. If outsourcing a task will cost less than your hourly rate, outsource it.
↓ Work as hard as you can. Even though who you work with and what you work on are more important than how hard you work.
↓ Become the best in the world at what you do. Keep redefining what you do until this is true.
↓ There are no get-rich-quick schemes. Those are just someone else getting rich off you.
↓ Apply specific knowledge, with leverage, and eventually you will get what you deserve.
↓ When you’re finally wealthy, you’ll realize it wasn’t what you were seeking in the first place. But that is for another day.

The first type is labor leverage, which means having others work for you. Labor leverage is one of the oldest forms of leverage, but in modern society, its effectiveness is not the best. [1] I even think it is the most outdated form of leverage. This is because managing other people is a very complex and challenging job that requires superb leadership skills. If done poorly, the manager might end up ostracized and devoured by their subordinates.

Capital is the second, relatively better form of leverage. Capital leverage means using money to expand the influence of decisions. [1] Capital is a more modern form of leverage, and utilizing capital leverage is somewhat difficult, requiring a certain skill set. In the 20th century, people achieved astonishing wealth by utilizing capital leverage. Capital leverage was the primary form of leverage in the 20th century. If you look at the wealthiest people, you will find that the richest are bankers and politicians in corrupt countries—they are essentially all people who can mobilize large amounts of capital. Look at the executives of large companies; besides tech companies, the CEOs of most established large companies are actually doing financial work. The amplifying effect of capital leverage is very obvious. Managing capital is easier than managing people because as capital continuously grows, the difficulty of managing it is far lower than managing an ever-expanding team.

The last type of leverage is the newest and the most accessible to ordinary people. This leverage is “products with zero marginal cost of reproduction.” This includes books, media, movies, and code. Among all leverages that can be used without needing permission from others, code is arguably the most powerful—it only requires a computer.
